This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2025-07-17 23:28:09 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/38769). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

[IMF Portwatch](https://portwatch.imf.org/), in partnership with the University of Oxford in the UK, offers satellite-based data on vessels to help users assess the impact of extreme events on global trade. Among the chokepoints it [monitors](https://portwatch.imf.org/pages/port-monitor) is the Strait of Hormuz, which is the only maritime passage from the Persian Gulf into the ocean. 

The Strait of Hormuz has long been the world's most important chokepoint for oil transit, from oil-rich Gulf states to the world's consumers of oil:

![](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/images/2012.01.04/Hormuz.png)(Source: the [US Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=4430))

Roughly 20% of the world's crude oil passes through the Strait each day. If shipping got cut off, it could have significant impact on the world's oil volumes and put sharp upward pressure on world energy prices. ([EIA](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65504))  

Amid the [Iran–Israel war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Israel_war), there were reports in June 2025 that Iran was considering closing the Strait, with a Persian-language media source headlined "If America goes to war with Iran, closing the Strait of Hormuz is our legitimate right." > This Iranian threat is not merely rhetorical, as the Iranian Navy and IRGC Navy have the capability to impose a blockade in the strait using asymmetric means like swarming with small, fast attack crafts equipped with cruise missiles and rockets, drones, naval mines, and coastal batteries of cruise and ballistic missiles of varying capabilities. In addition, Iranian naval forces also operate several frigates, corvettes, and submarines, which are also tasked to complement blockade efforts. Further compounding maritime risk is the presence of Iran’s two drone carriers—Shahed Bagheri and Shahed Madabi. These converted commercial vessels are capable of launching large drones, missiles, and helicopters, and thus also represent a significant strike capability for Iran at sea. Although the U.S. Fifth Fleet is based in Bahrain, which, along with allied naval assets, is positioned to respond against such blockade measures, any direct military engagement risks further escalating the conflict into a regional war.

**The Mystery of Iran’s Shadow Fleet: A Fleeting Light in the Gulf**
In mid-October 2025, 52 of Iran's 88 shadow fleet oil tankers suddenly activated their Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals simultaneously, revealing their locations across the Persian Gulf, Indian Ocean, and South China Sea for the first time in over seven years. This rare display of transparency—lasting only three days—contradicted Iran’s long-standing strategy of evading U.S. sanctions by hiding ship movements. The sudden activation, which coincided with the reactivation of UN sanctions under the 'snapback mechanism' and increased maritime enforcement by Malaysia, sparked speculation about its purpose. Analysts proposed three possible explanations: a defensive move to avoid legal justification for vessel seizures by demonstrating compliance with international maritime rules; a response to growing Chinese pressure requiring transparency for insurance and port access, as China accounts for over 80% of Iran’s oil exports; and an economic calculation to reduce logistical costs and increase revenue by avoiding the high expenses of the shadow fleet, including $100,000 daily VLCC rental fees, smuggling commissions, and losses from extended transit times. Despite the brief visibility, the fleet reverted to complete digital silence by October 17, 2025, leaving behind unresolved questions. Data from Kpler and TankerTrackers indicate Iran’s oil exports reached 1.95 million barrels per day in September 2025—its highest level since 2017—while production rose to 3.45 million barrels per day, surpassing Libya and Nigeria combined. Most Iranian oil is rerouted via intermediate tankers and processed in China’s independent 'small boiler refineries' to obscure its origin.

**Where is the Strait of Hormuz? Which city and country does it belong to?**
The Strait of Hormuz is a strategically vital waterway located between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, serving as the heart of global energy trade. Approximately 50 kilometers wide, it spans the narrowest point of the Arabian Peninsula, lying between the coastal regions of Iran and Oman. Geographically, it is a critical junction for maritime routes in western Asia. The strait has historically symbolized both trade and geopolitical power struggles, and today it remains one of the world’s most critical sea lanes, with millions of barrels of oil and natural gas tankers passing through daily. Known as the 'Gateway to the World's Energy,' the strait has been a focal point of control conflicts among seafaring nations throughout history. It is not confined to a single city but is bordered by key settlements: Bandar Abbas on the Iranian side, Iran’s largest port city and a major industrial and maritime trade hub, and Khasab on the Omani side, located on the Musandam Peninsula in northern Oman, known for its tranquil landscape.
